speechtext:
On the passage of the Act to providp for the marking- and inspection of packages containing fruit for sale, known as 1 The Fruit Alarks Act, 1901,' it became necessary to organize a staff for the administration and enforcement of the Act. The organization was placed, by the Minister of Agriculture, under the control of the Commissioner of Agriculture and Dairying, Dr. James W. Robertson, and became known as the fruit division of his branch.
In addition to the enforcement and administration of the Fruit Marks Act, the fruit division was charged with the supervision of the packing and transportation of fruit, particularly in cold storage and cool chambers, and the marketing of the same ; and this brought the work of the division in close connection with the cold storage and extension of markets divisions, which, having been organized principally for facilitating the transportation and promoting the sale of dairy products, were in charge of the chief of the dairy division, Air. J. A. Rud-dick, under the Commissioner of Agriculture and Dairying for several years prior to the retirement of the latter.

Ruddick was appointed dairy commissioner, the work of the cold storage and the extension of markets divisions being continued under him ; and owing to his close relations with the work of the fruit division, as above stated, it was deemed advisable to place the work of the latter division in his charge as well. speechtext:
Referring to himself.

was approached by the Deputy Minister of
Marine and Fisheries upon a certain date in this city with the specific inquiry as to the possible decision to be rendered in the case.
Let me point out the impropriety of the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, if this allegation is true, approaching a judge who was about to deliver a decision, to ask him which way that decision was likely to go. Captain Salmon adds :
In response to the inevitable and negative reply to such inquiry, the court was offered the suggestion that it might' be advisable to consult the counsel of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company, Mr. Archer, before rendering the decision, and that such action .would be exceedingly acceptable to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that it is not customary in this Canada of ours for orders to issue from ministers requesting judges to consult with counsel who may be engaged in an important case, before rendering judgment. It was evident that, through some inference probably, Mr. Archer concluded that Captain Salmon's judgment was not likely to be in favour of his clients, and consequently he deemed it expedient to take other measures, if possible, to keep the judgment from being delivered against the interest of the clients whom he represented. So it came about that Captain Salmon saw fit to give his resignation. He claimed that although as an officer of the department in ordinary matters he was bound to obey his superior officers, and when, on the demand of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, he was constituted a court of investigation, while he sat as



such court he was to all intents and purposes a judge, and could no longer be interfered with or unduly influenced until such time as he had delivered his decision. He considered that the attempt beforehand to ascertain his verdict, the attempt to delay his judgment, was certainly an attempt to hamper the usefulness of that court; and being an honourable and independant man, he felt there was but one of two things to do, either to disobey the orders that had proceeded from the department to which he belonged, or else to accept the orders, and to feel thereafter that in his capacity as a judge he had submitted to influences which he could not defend. And so he resigned his position, and he stated the reasons why he resigned, and it remains to be seen whether the reasons he gave are, by this House and the country, considered to be sufficient.
Now, I want simply to point out that to all intents and purposes Captain Salmon was a court. It is distinctly specified in the law that while constituted as a regular commissioner he is a court, and that therefore he was expected to uphold the dignity of the court, and endeavour to surround himself with the same atmosphere which should characterize any of the courts of this country. Captain Salmon resigned on the principle that our courts should be sacred and inviolate, that no man should be allowed, during the deliberation of the judge, to interfere with him in making up his mind. I may say that, speaking for the business and commercial interests of the great city of Montreal, it is a great disappointment to us that Captain Salmon should have found it necessary to resign and return to England. We had hoped that we might in time establish a Marine Court in Canada, whose decisions would be of equal value and importance to those of the Marine Courts on the other side of the Atlantic. We know that Captain Salmon in England would naturally state the reasons of his resignation, and naturally we feel that the Marine Courts of Canada will be degraded in the eyes of the mother country and of the world. Further than that, we feel that there are grave questions involved. When two great shipping companies meet with an accident and it becomes necessary to fix the responsibility of that accident upon the crew of one or other of these vessels, the possibility that undue influence may be brought to bear on the court in the interest of either of the contending parties, causes a feeling of doubt and of unprotectedness to exist throughout the entire shipping community. I would also point out that cases of this character where life and limb are at stake need to be considered with great care. In this particular case four lives had been lost. It was of course important that nothing should interfere with an absolutely impartial decision as to who was responsible for the Mr. AMES.
accident, and who was primarily responsible for that loss of life. The travelling public can never feel that they are protected until they are satisfied that when an investigation takes place it will be absolutely impartial.
Further than that, this case affects the marine and shipping interests of the city of Montreal. We are very anxious that it may become possible to reduce the amount of marine insurance that our shipping interests are called upon to pay. We realize that that can only be clone by creating, first of all, an excellent channel, and secondly, by creating confidence in the administration of everything connected with the operation of that channel. The doubt as to whether that duty will be well discharged, and as to whether justice will be impeded, militates against a reduction of the insurance which the shipping interests of Montreal are called upon to pay.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I trust that when the correspondence is brought down, and when we receive from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries the explanations which I am sure he will be willing to give, the apprehensions that have been aroused will be allayed. Certainly I think that this House, on the face of the case I have presented, is at least entitled to a full explanation and an opportunity to study the full correspondence.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
First of all I desire cordially to thank the hon. gentleman for having brought this question before the House, because, notwithstanding the explanations that have already been given in the newspapers and otherwise, there still seems to exist some misapprehension, either voluntary or involuntary. I do not mean to tax the hon. gentleman (l\rr. Ames) with having wrongfully represented the facts of the case, but surely the non. gentleman has not examined the law nor the facts as they have been published at various times in the newspapers. First, as regards the law. The hon. gentleman seems to be under the misapprehension, and has so stated, that Captain Salmon, when he was instructed to investigate the collision which occurred between the ' Canada ' and the ' Cape Breton,' was instructed to hold a court. That is quite erroneous and contrary to the law as it exists. First, I might state that there are two kinds of investigations held by the wreck commissioner under the authority of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. There is a preliminary investigation. Then, there is a formal investigation. The two are easy to understand with a few words of explanation. In this case there was no formal demand for an investigation. The two parties interested seemed to have thought that it was not required. After waiting for a few days or a few weeks I took it upon myself, in the

interest of the public and in the interest of navigation under section 4 of.l Edward VII, chap. 37, to instruct the wreck commissioner to proceed with a preliminary investigation.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext: What is the statute ?

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
1 Edward VII, chap. 37, an act to amend the Shipping Casualties Act, 1901, which was assented to on the 18th July, 1904. By section 4 I am empowered, as Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to order a preliminary investigation. The clause reads as follows :
The minister may appoint a principal officer of customs or any officer of the government of Canada, or any'person to make preliminary inquiries respecting such shipping casualties, and may define the territorial jurisdiction of any such officer or person.	*
Therefore, the person whom I might appoint is not designated, except that the person whom the minister designates is empowered to hold an investigation within the limits and according to the jurisdiction that the minister gives him and nothing else. Of course, it is provided by subsection 2 of section 4 how he is to conduct the inquiry and how he is to give his report upon it.
If, upon a preliminary inquiry, the officer holding it is of opinion that any loss, or damage, or the stranding of any ship, or any loss of life, has been caused by the wrongful act or default or by the incapacity of the pilot in charge, or that such pilot has been guilty of any gross act of misconduct or drunkenness, the license of such pilot may be suspended by such officer until a formal investigation under this act has been held and a further decision rendered upon the case :	provided that the
term of suspension shall not exceed a period of three days, unless the minister notifies such pilot within that time that a formal investigation will be held.
Captain Salmon held the investigation in virtue of this statute. He should have known it, and if he did not know it when he rendered judgment, and he seems not to have known it, he was unfit for the position he occupied.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.

speechtext: What is that ?

speechtext:
How are we to know that it was only a preliminary investigation What are the instructions ?
Mr. PREFONTAINE The papers will show it. I will place all the documents be-fere the House, and it will appear that it was a preliminary investigation that he was instructed to hold. From the beginning of the investigation I discovered that he was rather prejudiced against one or other of the parties, and I found it very strange indeed that this officer should stand in that position in an important case like this. So I directed him to carry out his proceedings properly and see that justice should be rendered to ail 13|
parties. Captain Sainton, knowing very well that he was not holding a formal investigation, never notified the parties as to what was the accusation. Instructions were given under the section I have just read to hold a preliminary investigation. Now, I go farther. Under this clause, I contend rightly, I presume, that the officer was under my charge during the whole time that he was conducting that investigation. I discovered that the parties interested refused to produce their witnesses and refused to take part in the investigation. The proprietors of the 'Cape Breton,' as well as the proprietors of the steamer 'Canada ' were interested in not taking part in the investigation, which was only a preliminary invesigation, end why? Because at the time that the in vestigation began there was pending before the Vice Admiralty Court of Quebec a case in which damages were claimed by the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Co., in which it was sought to establish the responsibility between the two companies and in which the two companies took part. The action uad been instituted, I understand, by the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Co. against the proprietors of the ' Cape Breton ' the Dominion Coal Company. This investigation had begun before Judge Routhier in the Vice Admiralty Court of Quebec, and both parties were fighting for their rights. In face of that what was my duty? My duty was clearly defined. It was to see that the rights of neither party should be prejudiced. 1 was informed by both sides that there were witnesses who would be examined before the Vice Admiralty Court and who would not appear before Captain Salmon in the preliminary investigation. I made Captain Salmon aware of that fact and I also gave him a formal notification that it might be necessary to suspend that investigation of his and await the judgment which would be pronounced in the Vice Admiralty Court. He went on with the investigation. Then it came to the point where the case in the Vice Admiralty Court had been argued before the judge. When the case had been argued before the judge I believed it was my duty to instruct Captain Salmon to suspend his proceedings, and that I did under the law. It is such a clear law that surely if it had been taken communication of by my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) he would not have made the remarks he has made. All through the Act, chapter 33 of 1 Edward VII., 1901, it is clearly established that the wreck commissioner in conducting a formal investigation remains under the control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in order that justice may be rendered properly. Following up what I have said just now, I will cite section 15 of the Shipping Casualties Act of 1901.
Whenever a formal investigation is likely to involve a question as to cancelling or susnend-ing the certificate of competency or service of any master, mate or engineer, he shall be fur-

nished before the commencement of the investigation with a copy of the report or statement of the case upon which the investigation has been ordered.
In this case none was furnished anybody ; there was no complaint on the part of the families of those who had lost their lives in the accident, for the simple reason that coroners' inquiries had been held in each case a long time before the date of this preliminary investigation which was held by Mr. Salmon.
Then I would cite section 14.
Every formal investigation shall be conducted in such manner that ' if a charge is made against any person, that person shall have an opportunity of making a defence.
Following the well known English principle, that nobody shall be found guilty or condemned without being heard.
Now I cite from the same Act, clause 22.
The minister may, if he thinks that the justice of the case requires it, re-issue and return the Canadian certificate of the master, mate or engineer which has been cancelled or suspended or shorten the time for which it is suspended, or grant in place thereof a certificate of the same or any other lower grade.
Therefore again the minister remains the final tribunal in the case when it is a formal investigation, and in this case it was not a formal investigation.
Then we have section 25.
to any case where a formal investigation has been held the minister may order the investigation to be re-heard either generally or as to any part thereof ; and he shall do so-[DOT]
(a) If new and important evidence which could not he produced at the investigation has been discovered.
What was the necessity I would like to know of Oapt. Salmon, an officer of my department, of pronouncing a judgment when I was instructing him to hear the witnesses that had been heard before the Vice-Admiralty Court.

That statement is exactly true. Capt. Salmon had not given satisfaction; there had been very serious complaints against him and without going beyond this case I need only cite one incident with reference to one of the officers of the ' Cape Breton.' I shall not quote from papers on this side of the water but I shall cite the Edinburgh ' Scotsman,' in which the following remarks are made as regards the conduct of this individual :	'	.
The Merchant Service Guild and Shipping Inquiries in Canada.
The conduct of marine inquiries into shipping casualties held in Canada has lately been once more taken in hand by the Merchant Service Guild. It has been urged that captains and officers have been bullied and brow-beaten whilst under evidence, and that the decisions of these inquiries have not been in accord with justice. A recent case which the Guild dwelt upon was that of the investigation into the collision between the steamers ' Canada ' and ' Cape Breton.' The chief officer of the latt'er steamer, whilst under evidence, was subjected to a searching examination in the rules of the road by the president of the court. Captain Salmon, who also held the position of Canadian wreck commissioner. In the course of his examination the officer gave an answer which the Guild considered a.s a perfectly correct one, hut the president, thinking otherwise, his anger became aroused and he ejaculated that ' it was God's mercy that he bad not had an accident previously, and that the place for him was in jail.'
Having ascertained the facts, the Guild communicated with the Minister of Marine, Canada, referring to this unwarrantable and offensive statement and requesting Captain Salmon to make an apology for the insult offered to the chief officer of the ' Cape Breton.' The reply of the Minister of Marine stated that Captain Salmon had resigned his position as wreck commissioner. but that the communication of the Guild had been filed for reference if necessary. Subsequently, it transpired that, although he had nothing to do with the collision, the certificate of the chief officer of the 'Cape Breton' had been withheld by the Court of Inquiry until such
time as he had been examined by an examiner of masters and mates, and found efficient in the rules of the road. The Guild again communicated with the authorities, stating that if would be an extraordinary thing that the court should deal with the certificate of a witness simply because of the manner in which he gave his evidence. They knew of no legal authority which permitted the certificate being withheld, and trusted that this decision would be quashed. They have now received a further letter from the Canadian Minister of Marine, who conveys his best thanks for information furnished him as to practises of the Board of Trade in connection with inquiries into shipping casualties, and alse begs to state for the information of the Guild that the certificate of the chief officer of the * Cape Breton ' has been returned to him.
Captain 'Salmon had no more jurisdiction over this man than the man in the moon, and had no power to suspend his certificate except for three days; and if during those three days the Minister of Marine and Fisheries did not give the necessary notice that there would be a formal inquiry, the certificate would have to be returned. Captain Salmon did not know that. He was determined to act as a court of justice, and committed the wrongful act that he did. I have heard of a commissioner's court in my native county which condemned a witness, and this is a case of the same kind. In the province of Quebec these commissioners have jurisdiction in small cases to the extent of $25. These gentlemen live amongst the farming community, but they generally know a little more than their neighbours. In the case I refer to and of which I am reminded by Captain Salmon's action, a butcher was suing one of his neighbours for an account of $10 for meat. The farmer contended that he did not owe the account, and the plaintiff brought as a witness the hired man of the farmer, who had lived in the house of the farmer at the time the meat had been furnished. The witness said: I know that this meat has been furnished, and that the account is correct, because I ate the meat myself. The justice said : You ate the meat, then ? The man who eats the meat pays for it-judgment against the witness.' That case was appealed to the higher court in Montreal and it cost about $200 to quash that judgment of the justice of the peace. The action of Captain Salmon in this case has been just the same. He condemned this officer and cancelled his certificate because he did not as a witness give an answer that was satisfactory to Captain Salmon. The position taken by Captain Salmon was entirely wrong, unjust and unfair, and revealed an incapacity on his part which it is hardly possible to imagine. As regards his resignation, as I stated in my interview, if it had not been tendered he would have been asked for it, because he was unfit for the position he occupied. As regards the poor fellow returning to England, that is not exactly the fact. Captain Salmon cannot get a position under any marine organization; I know that

perfectly well. He is in New York at the present time. I do not want to say any more about him. The certificates of the officers which have been cancelled, like that of the first mate of the ' Cape Breton,' have been returned to them. We could not hold the officers as suspended, and it was our duty to do what we have done in the matter. I repeat, if Captain Salmon had known his duties, if he had known the law that he was administering, he would not have rendered himself guilty of the act which he committed. I thank the hon. gentleman for having given me the occasion to state the facts as they are. The documents will be willingly placed before the House as soon as possible within the next few days, and they will bear out exactly what I have stated.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext: After the discussion which has taken place this afternoon, the members of the House will be curious to see the documents and to find out exactly what Captain Salmon's position was. I have not the pleasure of Captain Salmon's acquaintance. In fact, my estimate of him has been formed from what I think I heard from the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries himself, a couple of years ago, when, in passing his estimates through this House, ho gave unstinted praise to that individual, declaring him to be highly qualified for the position he held.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I did not know him then.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend did not know him he should not have gone so far as he did at that time. But my hon. friend has drawn a distinction to-day which has never been drawn before, and which I think he himself neglected to draw, when there was a great storm in the press of the city of Montreal and among the public generally, as to the action of the Department of Marine and Fisheries towards Captain Salmon. I have listened to the reading of the interview which my hon. friend gave to the ' Star ' at that time, and in which he failed entirely to point out that Captain Salmon was holding what he calls a preliminary inquiry. The matter was discussed at great length in the papers of the city of Montreal at the time. My hon. friend will remember that a great deal of indignation was shown at the interference with Captain Salmon in the performance of his statutory duties. Nobody that I am aware of claimed that Captain Salmon was not holding a court. On that point I think there cannot be any doubt. In fact, the Department of Marine and Fisheries and my hon. friend the minister himself cannot have considered that Captain Salmon has proceeded under the section of the Shipping Casualties Act of 1901, which he has quoted to the House, because if that was the case, why did the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries-and that has not Mr. PREFONTAINE,
been contradicted-say that Captain Salmon was holding a court, and endeavour to persuade him from rendering judgment, and suggest to him that he should see Mr. Archer in order to satisfy the desire of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and learn from Mr. Archer what he should do ? It has not been contended at any time that Captain Salmon was acting under the section referred to by my hon. friend. There are two kinds of inquiry, one of an informal nature, and the other, which is the one undoubtedly held in this case, under a section to which I will refer in a moment. But what I submit to this House is this, that even if that inquiry had been held under section 4 of the Shipping Casualties Act of 1901, as amended in 1904, it -was not proper for the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or his depart' ment in any way to interfere with the wreck commissioner in the execution of his duties in a preliminary inquiry. To suppose that even in a preliminary inquiry, the wreck commissioner, who is seized with that inquiry and is proceeding with it, may be dictated to by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries-to suppose that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may order the wreck commissioner to stop the inquiry, is, I submit, entirely contrary to the very words and sense of the Casualties Act of 1901. I have no doubt that the instructions to the wreck commissioner, will show that he was not acting under section 4 at all, but section 8. Let me read that section 8 as amended by the statute, chap. 64, 3 Edward VII., 1903 :
The minister may appoint any officer of the government of Canada, or any judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec, or any judge of a county count, or any local judge in Admiralty of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or any stipendiary magistrate, to be a commissioner to hold formal investigations, and a commissioner shall for such purposes be a court.
Among the cases in which such court may hold a formal investigation of cases of shipping casualties and collisions, I venture to assert, without fear of contradiction, that Oapt. Salmon proceeded under that section 8. He did not proceed under section 4 which calls upon him merely to make a preliminary inquiry and report to the minister whether a formal investigation is necessary.. There never was before the commissioner any question as to the nature of the investigation he was holding. It was treated as a formal investigation, and the commissioner presiding was considered the judge. All parties interested appeared before him, and all the proceedings were conducted, as they should have been, under section 8. The proposition of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that because an action was begun before the Admiralty Court was a sufficient reason to warrant his stopping this investigation, seems to me absolutely without foundation.

The object of the proceedings in the Admiralty Court was to settle the question of damages due by one shipping company to the other. That court sat for the purpose of settling a private claim affecting private interests and not at all as a tribunal to settle matters affecting the public interest. But the court over which Capt. Salmon presided is one that was created by statute in the interests of shipping generally, in the public interest, for the purpose of inquiring into the causes of the accident, according to the rules of marine science, and reporting the results to the department. After an accident has taken place and a formal investigation into the causes of that accident has begun, to suppose that because the parties interested judged lit to bring their difficulties before the Admiralty' Court, the" commissioner may be subjected to an order from the Department of Marine and Fisheries to stop his proceedings, is to defeat completely the object of this legislation. The preteu-sion of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that, under all circumstances and at any time, a commissioner is subject to the orders of his department appears to me absolutely repugnant to any wise and proper interpretation of the Casualties Act. Whether the commissioner were holding a mere preliminary inquiry or making a formal investigation under section 8 he was not subject to orders from the Minister of Marine. I am sure that a careful reading of the authorities quoted by my hon. friend will only prove that the wreck commissioner may under special circumstances, such as when new witnesses or new evidence have been discovered be ordered to renew or reopen his inquiry. The facts of this case, as they have hem stated by my hon. friend from St. Antoine Division (Mr. Ames) and as they will no doubt be shown by the papers when brought down, show that the minister went a step further and considered himself authorized to prevent that investigation. I think that in so doing he assumed an authority which does not belong to him, and that this House should not fail to express its appreciation of such conduct.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
In rising for the first time, Mr. Speaker, to address this House I regret very much that I have to differ from my hon. friend the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), and the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). The sad accident to the steamers ' Cape Breton ' and 'Canada' is one of course in which I felt a very deep interest, and the proceedings in connection with which I followed, as it was my duty, from step to step. As far as I am in a position to form a judgment, in my opinion, the course taken by the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was legal and right and gave justice to both parties. When I say that his action was legal, I am not speaking from any legal knowledge
of my own, but according to the advice received from eminent counsel-not alone from Mr. Archer, who was our attorney in the matter, but also from counsel who are acting with him, namely, Mr. Pentland and Mr. Wm. Cook, of Quebec, and Mr. Angers- not my predecessor in this House, but the Hon. Mr. Angers. And I think I may safely say that Messrs. Pentland, Cook and Angers, are recognized throughout the Dominion as the best marine lawyers in this country. This accident took place late in June of last year. A few weeks later, the wreck commissioner held an inquiry. In that investigation, the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company decided not to take any part, as we could not get hold of all the witnesses we required. We instituted an action in the Vice-Admiralty Court in the city of Quebec ; and while the case was proceeding in that court, Capt. Salmon, to my knowledge, came down into the corridor of the Court House of the city of Quebec and there threatened our lawyers that he would render judgment that same morning, and he made that threat in the presence of the witnesses of both parties who were in the corridor. In view of this extraordinary conduct, I, acting for the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company, got our counsel together and asked them what could be done to save the situation, as no doubt it was the intention of Capt. Salmon to prejudice all these witnesses. Aftqr asking Capt. Salmon without success to withhold his judgment, the Hon. Mr. Angers advised our attorney, Mr. Archer, as a last resource, to see the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as he had a perfect right to do, and ask him to request Capt. Salmon to wait. The hon. minister was then at the Frontenac Hotel, and the request was only a fair and reasonable one, and in granting it the minister did nothing but justice to both parties. Since that ex parte enquete before Capt. Salmon-an enquete in which the Richelieu Company was not represented-took place, the Vice-Admiralty Court gave judgment. We are told that this is a civil suit and nothing else. But if the Richelieu company or any other party are civilly responsible for any damages, surely they must be criminally responsible as well for the lives of these people. One reason why we thought Capt. Salmon was unfit for the position he held was that he did not even know the local law of the port of Sorel. There was a law for the port of Sorel, but there was no law defending the limits of that port that we might know exactly where that .local law applied. That is the reason why we did not appear before Capt. Salmon's court. This is not a political question and I feel free to differ from my hon. confrere (Mr. Ames), to state that difference frankly, and to say that, in my opinion, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries showed only justice and fair play to both parties in this case.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not know wliat was called for by considerations of justice between the parties, but, as to the action of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the case, this House can have but one opinion. The minister said he was gratified that the hon. member for St. Antoine, Montreal (Mr. Ames), brought the subject before the House as it gave him an opportunity of showing how innocent he and the department were in the whole transaction. Yet he did not tell us whether this was a preliminary or a formal investigation. This could be shown by bringing down the Instructions given to the officer who investigated the case. Yet he has not brought down those instructions.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL AND P. E. I. RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The minister spoke in defence of his action and said he had all the papers here. Yet, he did not quote the instructions to show whether this was a preliminary or a formal investigation. But the thing for the House to consider is not the merits of the case, but the interference by the minister with an officer, be he judge or otherwise, who was authorized by statute to investigate a casualty case. What difference does it make, as my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has said, taking the statement of the minister himself, whether this was a preliminary investigation or a formal one. What business had the minister or his deputy to interfere or make suggestions as to what evidence [DOT]should be taken? The statute sets forth in a peremptory manner the duties and powers of an officer making a preliminary inquiry in such a case. He can inspect the ship; he can inspect premises, having the right of entry; he can summon witnesses and swear them; he can look into documents; he can allow expenses to the witnesses and inflict penalties upon those who refuse to give evidence. He is to report his opinion upon the case, accompanied with such extracts from the evidence as he sees fit. So. even if it were a preliminary investigation, it was the duty of the officer to investigate and report to the minister. Fancy a minister, when such an investigation is going on, suggesting that some other evidence should be submitted or that the officer should not give his report with reference to the matter. Why cannot the minister tell us whether it was a preliminary or a formal investigation and remove all doubt? My hon. friend from .Jacques Gar-tier says it is clear that not a question was raised in the court as to the formal nature of the investigation. In such an investigation the statute provides what the duties of the officer are, and a reading of them wall show that the reference was the same as sending the case to a court of justice to be inquired into. The minister says that if it were the preliminary inquiry, the penalty Mr. FORGET.
that the officer could inflict was a suspension of the officers for three days, pending decision of the question of holding a formal inquiry. If that is all that was involved, why was there any necessity for the minister or his deputy to interfere? As to the merits of the case I know nothing. Captain Salmon may be right or he may be wrong in his finding. But one thing is plain and undeniable, and that is that there has been tampering by the minister or his deputy with an inquiry ordered under statute. The minister brings evidence, intended to excuse himself by showing that the commissioner was unfit for the position to which he had been appointed. Why, this officer was selected by the minister bimself to investigate this case. And what is the evidence that he brings to justify his dismissal of the officer? Letters furnished to him after the dismissal. And fancy the mean insinuation of the minister that this officer, who, presumably was doing what he thought to be his duty, is now a vagrant in the streets of New York. And when he said this there was a laugh from his supporters. What is the inference? There is no inference possible except that this is a warning to all officers of the department whose duty it is to hold such investigations as this:	Do not dare to exercise an independent judgment, for the minister may differ with you in opinion, and the result will be that you will become a wanderer in the streets of New York.

speechtext:
I believe that as a mover of the motion I am entitled to say a word in reply before the debate is closed. There seems to be considerable doubt in the minds of the minister and of the House as to whether this was a formal inquiry or a preliminary inquiry. Certain it is that Captain Salmon thought it was a formal inquiry, because as I understand the minister' to say, that if it had been a preliminary inquiry the maximum penalty he would have been permitted to impose was three days suspension of license. You have only to read his report to see that he considered himself empowered to enforce a penalty far in excess of three days suspension of license. The penalties that he permitted himself to inflict under a formal investigation shows that in his judgment it was a formal investigation. For example, he takes upon himself to suspend the certificate of Captain St. Louis. I doubt if he would have cancelled the certificate if he had considered the investigation a preliminary one. He also suspends for a period of twelve calender months the certificate of Peter Kane ; would he have done so if he had considered the investigation merely a preliminary one ? You have only to read the entire judgment of Captain Salmon to see that he thought he was carrying out a formal investigation. As we have endeavoured to follow the minister through his ex-

planations, we have noted that he is culling flowers On both sides of the path ; that whenever any reference seems to assist him on the ground that it was a preliminary investigation he claims the right to that reference; and whenever there is a reference which seems to help him in the contention that it was a formal investigation, he also claims that as well. There is one thing I would like very much to know, and that is, how it was that the minister discovered that Captain Salmon was prejudiced against one of the parties. The minister says he saw there was about to be a miscarriage of justice. How did he find that out ? Now, Mr. Speaker, I admit that the minister has the right, after judgment has been delivered and he thinks there has been a miscarriage of justice, to reverse the decision and to remit the penalties. But I submit that during the course of the enquete, while the judge is preparing to deliver his decision, the minister has no right to interfere on the presumption that the court is prejudiced against one of the parties concerned. I would like to point out also that the instructions which were given by the department to the wreck commissioner, if we are to judge from those which were given to his successor, Captain Spain, are very formal. We have only to turn to the last report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries to read : ' That the minister may appoint a commissioner to hold formal investigations and these are the instructions which were given to Captain Spain, which we find in his report of December 6, 1904 :
My instructions are to investigate every casualty, and to deal promptly with any carelessness or want of judgment showp by either pilots or shipmasters in the navigation of Canadian waters.
' To investigate every casualty and to deal promptly.' That does not mean to withhold judgments indefinitely. The minister has also seen fit to state that Captain Salmon has fallen from grace, and that he is a character no longer to be received with confidence or to be given any further opportunity of dispensing judgments here in Canada. Admitting that is the present opinion of the minister, I am sorry to see that he was so woefully deceived when he appointed him. On the 9th of October, 1903, he told the House in Committee of Supply :
Last year we inaugurated a system of holding investigations into every casualty that occurred. The members of the committee will recollect that this was done at the special request of the Board of Trade in England, in order to render the service as effective as possible. . . . We have replaced Captain Smith, deceased, by Captain Reginald Salmon', at a salary of $2,000. This department is being thoroughly reorganized under a very able officer and we try to make it as effective as possible. Captain Salmon is an officer of the Royal Navy Reserve holding the rank of lieutenant. .	.	* Captain Salmon is
a commissioner of investigation under the law and he has associated with him two expert assessors. . . . We have had a great deal of difficulty in finding a man qualified as Captain Salmon is to take the position at $2,000. It was only after a good deal of inquiry in Canada and England that we succeeded in getting Captain Salmon. He had been employed in Canada on the surveys by the British government, and he became attached to Canada and accepted the position.
Poor man ! He became attached before he knew the ways of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
But I intend, under the advice of Captain Salmon, who is a very efficient officer, to have this matter gone into thoroughly, and have efficient schools of navigation established .at the proper ports.
Surely he must have been a good man when his advice was taken by the department in the establishment of naval schools; but now we regret to find that his services are lost to the country for ever.

I think the minister was giving us a list of the increases in Nova Scotia.

I think I gave the gross amount of the increase. In Nova Scotia it amounted to $2,210. Of these 37 increases, I may say that 24 were in Halifax, one in Annapolis, one in Canso, one in Digby, two in Lunenburg, four in North Sydney, one in Pictou, one in Port Hawkesbury, and two in Sydney.

Salaries and travelling expenses of inspectors of ports and of other officers on inspection and preventive service, including salaries and expenditure in connection with the Board of Customs and for the compiling of statistical returns of imports and exports, $189,200.
Will the minister explain very briefly his system of inspection ?

The inspection is carried on by officers duly appointed, one in New Brunswick, who also takes Prince Edward Island, two in Nova Scotia, two in Quebec, five in Ontario, one in British Columbia, one in Manitoba, who takes in the Territories, and the collector of customs at Dawson, who has supervision as inspector over Whitehorse. Their duties are to be continually engaged in the inspection of the offices, examining the clerical work and everything in connection with the business of the office. They report to the commissioner of customs as to the condition of each port. If anything improper is reported, that of course has to be taken cognizance of by the commissioner, it is brought under my notice and has to be dealt with. The Inspection is now pretty thorough. Before 1896, owing to the illness of some of the inspectors, it had been impossible to inspect some of the offices for three or four years and some things went wrong, but in 1896 under the old government Mr. McKay was appointed and since then Mr. Boultbee has died and his place has been filled. I think I can safely say that now
every port in inspected once a year if not more frequently.
What members of the Board of Inspection or the staff of inspectors are in Ottawa ?

Is Mr. MeMichael one of the Ontario inspectors or is he a chief ?
He is the chief inspector.

Yes, he is the head and he looks after all the others.
Mr. FOSTER, Do the reports of the others go to him ?
Yes, they are all forwarded through him.
What does he do with reference to these reports ? Does he give them a thorough going over ?
Yes, he goes through them, makes a report and sends them to the commissioner.

I wanted to get the modus operand! When Mr. MeMichael gets the reports of the inspectors what authority has he? Does he deal with any portion of them himself, and is there a certain time in which he has to report to the commissioner, or does he simply report upon and forward all these reports to the commissioner. I want to ascertain if any of these reports fall by the way or any portion of them, or do they all come to the commissioner with the advantage of the chief inspector's notes hnd comments.

Yes, they all come to the commissioner here and final action is taken here. Mr. MeMichael would not take action himself, but he would draw the attention of the commissioner to anything which he thought necessary. The commissioner, however, would have to take action.
Mr. FOSTER, Does the commissioner take the sole action in conjunction with his minister of course, or have you a board here, which assists in any way.

No, not in reference to that matter, because these inspectors are doing the initial part of the work, and it becomes a matter of judgment whether a search should be made. If a shortage were discovered, as sometimes happens, we would have to take a step which we do not like to take, and perhaps feel it incumbent upon

us to relieve the officer of his position. Since I have been at the head of the department we have changed the practice. Formerly we took securities from private individuals, but now the officers are all under guarantee companies, so that if there is any shortage, we simply notify the insurance company which gives the guarantee, and have nothing more to do with the matter. The company has to make the loss good.
How are sub-collect-oi f paid-by salary or commission ? If by salary, is there any uniform rule ?

They are paid by salary, invariably I think. But at certain small points, which are not customs ports, for convenience we give postmasters the power to collect in small matters, and allow them 10 per cent commission.

There have been cases in which goods have been brought to the sub-agency, and a man at the place has been employed as an agent of the owner of goods, and has charged a certain fee, and the sub-collector, in stating the amount of duty which the individual had to pay, has included the agents' fee. I myself have seen an account rendered by a sub-collector at Neepawa, in which a fee of 50 cents was charged as the agent's commission on an article on which there was paid $4 of duty. It seems to me that that is entirely outside of the duties of a collector.

So it is. While brokers may do business for others, we do not recognize them in any way at all. They are not agents of the department. If any charge is made by them, it is no part of our duty to collect it.
The party could not get the goods released without paying the agent's fee. The sub-collector has no right to constitute himself an agent for the collection of the agent's fee.
No, certainly not. We have had occasion to point out that if people pay that, it is not on the demand of the Department of Customs at all.

Another thing occurred in connection with the same office. A person bringing in household effects from the old country was anxious to have them passed immediately, but could not produce his certified invoice in order to get the benefit of the preferential rate. He asked the sub-collector of customs if, by paying the full amount of the duty, and later on producing the certified invoice, he would get a rebate. The sub-collector replied, No, certainly not.

That would be a misapprehension of his duties, because that is our course. If a person comes with an invoice not properly certified, our regulations provide, and our officers are so instructed, Mr. PATERSON.
that the goods are to be allowed in at the full general tariff rate, and when the proper invoice is produced, a rebate is allowed.
And there is no time specified ?	.
No time specified, except that it has to be done within three years.
Is there any age at which the hon. minister deems it right or proper to superannuate officials of his department in the outside service ?

Under the general Superannuation Act a person over 60 years of age may be superannuated, as the' hon. gentleman knows. We have many officers over that age who are capable of performing their duties, and who do not wish to be superannuated.
May I ask the minister if the case of Mr. George Watson, the collector of customs at Collingwood, who is in his 77th year, is now under consideration for superannuation ?
I think he has not asked for it.
He has been upwards of 40 years in the service. Can the minister recollect whether or not he has applied for superannuation ?
Not that the accountant is aware of.
I do not think the accountant would be aware of it. I want to know if the minister is aware of it.
No, I am not.
There is no question of his superannuation or the appointment of his successor before the minister at present?
No, not at present, so far as I remember. Is there a feeling that he is not able to discharge his duties ?

No, but it was felt about the time of the election that it was very expedient to have him superannuated on account of the government receiving the very warm services of a gentleman who was to receive the position. The minister never heard of that ?
Oh, no.
I think he will soon hear of it.
That is certainly an age at which a gentleman might ask to be relieved from service.
I think so, and in view of the services the other gentleman gave, I think it would perhaps be quite right for him to receive the position.

Well, I do not know
who the other gentleman is.

I wish to ask the minister how the payment for overtime comes about. At the port of Sarnia you have paid for overtime during the past year $2,786. which is distributed over a number of names. How is the time computed ?

They are paid so much an hour. Up to two years ago a large part of that amount was paid by the transportation companies. The department and the House, however, took the view that it was only proper that, as the revenue was collected by our officers, they should be paid by us. Therefore we have assumed the payment or all overtime, and do not any longer charge it to the transportation companies ; but if the transportation companies ask for the services of our officers on Sundays, which happens in some rare cases, we do not pay for that; the transportation companies have to bear it. Is the hon. gentleman's question how we divide it among the different officers ?
I want to know how "ou can check it among the different officers.

They must serve so many hours, and the collector must certify to the fact. The work must be done before 8 o'clock in the morning or after 6 o'clock at night, and in every case they must state the amount of overtime they have put in. The collector has to certify the account, and they are paid 25 cents an hour.
As regards the expenses of the inspectors, on what basis are they regulated?
The actual travelling and reasonable living expenses for which they furnish vouchers.
How many revenue cruisers does the minister employ?

Really only one is under customs. In Cape Breton waters during the summer we engage a boat called the ' Gladiator.' We have many revenue cutters but they are under the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Under whose authority do they work. The Customs or Marine?
The officers are wholly under my department and are under Mr. Jones. The repairs are done through the Marine Department but are charged against us.
What are the duties of the Board of Customs ?

They decide questions that are not very clear under the law. For instance, as to whether a certain article might be a woollen or a cotton. They
have periodical meetings at which they rule upon the different questions referred to them. When a decision of theirs is approved by a Minister of Customs, he signs it, and it has the authority of law, but it is subject to an appeal to the Governor in Council.
Are the statistical officers all in Ottawa ?

Yes, fifty-seven. They are not all new. Under the old system they would be at Montreal and other ports. They get out reports every month giving us as complete information as you will find in the Trade and Navigation returns.
The work which was formerly done at the out ports by those who were removed to Ottawa is not now being done there?
No, it is done here.
But all the data for that work has to be fro warded from those ports?
Yes.
That does not add very much to the work of those ports? The minister does not duplicate by appointing men to fill the vacancies caused by removal of statistical officers to Ottawa?

We did not fill the vacancies where men were engaged at large ports exclusively in this statistical work. But in so small ports, like Guelph or Brantford, where men were engaged partly in this work and partly in other work, we could not reduce the staff by the removal of one officer. But the increase in the business has generally justified keeping the staff up to what it was before.

As to these monthly reports, I would be glad if the minister would tell us whether business men really value and appreciate them. My impression is that they are not much called for or used. But the reports would be much more interesting to me, I know-and I pay attention to the trade and navigation returns-if a column were added to these monthly reports giving the amount of revenue collected. It may be that these reports cost more than they are worth, but, if it is well to continue them, I would suggest that they would be exactly in the form of the trade and navigation returns.
Can the minister say what the expense of publishing these monthly reports is ?
We have not that separately from our other printing.

Perhaps the minister would get that information. I confess it looks well to have monthly reports, but, as my hon. friend from Ilalton (Mr. Henderson) says they may not be of enough use to justify

the expense of printing and distribution. 1 hope the minister will be able to tell us at a future sitting what the ordinary monthly circulation is and give us some idea of the expense.
iMr. PATERSON. This system of monthly report was established at the request of the Manufacturer's Association. Perhaps a merchant or ordinary business man may not value them much. But every one doing or contemplating an export business finds them of value. We have to do a great deal of this work any way in order to get out our yearly report. And it is always to be remembered that statistics in order to be of value must be fresh, tinder the old system we were not able to get out the fiscal returns for the year ending June 30, until the February or March following, when the figures were of little or no value. Now the figures are fresh and they actually help and facilitate trade. So while it involves an expense I think the expense is justified by the good done to the trade of the country at large. It may be that comparatively few business men in the country subscribe or take an interest in them, but the trade that is helped by them is large and important.
How many employees are there in the Customs Department in the Yukon ? 'There is a vote of $42,000 for that.
There are 12 at Dawson and 11 at Whitehorse, the out-port.
This covers the salaries of all ?
Salaries and expenses.
What has been the method of the Customs Department so far as living allowance is concerned ?

It was thought better to pay salaries and living allowance so that if the cost of living went down there might be a reduction without a reduction of salary. Formerly we paid $150 per month living allowance. Now, we pay the married men $1,500 a year and the single men $1,000.

I see an item in tonight's paper headed ' Will have to send for Wives.' It says :	,
An order was issued yesterday in the administration building to the effect that all married men whose wives live1 outside the Territory should have $25 a month cut off their living allowance.
I gather that, for years officers have been drawing a living allowance as for the whole family though their wives and families have been living outside the territory. The Department of the Interior at least seems to have found this out.
If a man is keeping, his family at one place and boarding in another I do not know that he gains much by it.
Has there been any revision of the allowances since it was first fixed?
It was $1,800, and is now $1,500 for married men and $1,000 for single men. Formerly it was $1,800 all round, no distinction made.

I would call to the hon. gentleman's attention something which I find in the Ottawa ' Free Press ' of tonight-I do not know if there is any authority for it:
An order was issued yesterday in the administration building to the effect that all married men whose wives live outside the Territory should have $25 a month cut off their living allowance.
I understand from my hon. friend that married men get so much and single men so much. This report says :
Formerly married men received an allowance of $125 a month for living expenses. Now only the married men whose wives are with them will get this amount. The others will get but $100. _
They are treated like single men when their wives are not there.
It is said that a couple of men whose salaries are affected by this order to the tune of $300 a year have telegraphed for their wives to come in at once. As yet it is not known how many men in the service this new order will affect. The heads of the departments will report on the matter and will tell how many men under them are married but whose wives are not with them.
Has my hon. friend any knowledge of this in his department ?
No ; I do not think that refers to the Customs Department.

I think all the departments having officers in the Yukon should adopt some like plan. There seems to be a different way of treating these men in the different departments. In the Department of Justice they are treated the best of all, and in other departments they are not all treated alike.

When you go into the legal profession, they are not governed by the ordinary laws. As concerns the Post Office, the Interior and the Customs departments, my impression is that we are all about on the same basis. I think, so far as those three departments are concerned, the living allowance is about on the same basis. At any rate, we have reduced ours from $1,800 to $1,500 for married men, and then make a distinction for the first time between married and single men.

Whether his wife is
there or not ?
Of course, if the man is married, we assume that his wife will be with him. But sometimes they go into that country on temporary business. I know

the collector at Dawson has his family with him, although he himself is out just now. There are some single men there. I fancy that other officers have their wives with them. I do not know about the appraiser, he goes to Victoria ; there is no use keeping him at Dawson all winter, and his living allowance is cut off when he is in Victoria. I presume his family is with him in Victoria.
What proportion of the minister's officials are uniformed ?
I think all who come in contact with the public at stations as landing waiters.	.
Are the uniforms furnished by the department ?
I think they have to provide themselves once a year. We make an allowance of $8 once a year for the uniform. They buy the cap, and we supply the cap band and the buttons for the uniform.
Have they to get these uniforms at any particular place ?
No.
You take care that the uniforms are uniform-that your officers present a uniform appearance ?
Yes. it is rather a neat uniform ; it is certainly a great improvement on the former one.
You don't have to make any contracts, then ?
No.
There is an item here of $12,474.65, which seems to be taken from the general expenditure and which is paid by the railways. What is that ?

That is a refund of money paid by transportation companies. In 1903 the committee of the House authorized the Department of Customs to pay their own officers. If you recognize the fact that trains should be allowed to run in the general interest of the country, it is part of our business to pay officers who are to collect the revenue for the Dominion of Canada. It involves asking for $60,000 or $80,000 more, and I hesitated for two or three years. But we take the position that we will not pay for, overtime on Sunday, that if you are going to require men to work on Sunday you will have to pay for that. In this amount you find there are sums that are refunded to us by the transportation companies.
The revenue that you collect on Sunday, do you take that into the funds ?
The Sunday work they require to do is entering and clearing vessels, not to collect the revenue.
No revenue collected on Sunday ?
I said the principal work is entering and clearing vessels. We do not encourage, in fact we discourage, any Sunday work that can be avoided.
But the money which is collected on Sunday goes into the treasury of the Dominion ?
If there is any collected.
But as a matter of fact the sum is collected ?
I could not say that. I think it is very doubtful.

The hon. minister sees that he is running up against a place where he cannot find an argument, because, if he takes the revenues which he collects on Sundays, on the ground that he himself has laid down he is bound to pay the expenses for collecting the revenues on Sunday as well as on any other day. We will not pursue that point.
I discouraged Sunday work as much as possible. '
The hon. minister himself does not work on Sunday.
No, I do not.
And when it is done you do not pay for it.
Well, I suppose we have discussed this item enough now.
As far as I am concerned I am satisfied.	*
The whole item is carried is it not?
All right.
We might as well call it six o'clock.
All right. What will be taken up to-night ?
We are ready to go on with militia, I suppose, if the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence tSir Frederick Borden) is here.
You must look after your minister.
I know, but I was asking the hon. gentleman. I think the Auditor General's Report in reference to that is down.
Yes, 'Militia and Defence' is down.

Very well, we will go on with that.

The minister might explain the large increase in this item.

Before going on with these estimates I would like to make a suggestion to the committee, and to my hon. friends opposite. I would suggest that the same course might be pursued this year as we have been pursuing for the last two or three years, namely, to agree upon a day on which the main discussion of the state of the militia should take place, and that in the meantime some progress might he made with the items here, with the understanding that when that discussion takes place, any subject covered by any of these items should be open to discussion.

If anything is to be done at all that will have to be the way because the minister's report, I understand, is not yet down. We will go over these items and the minister will be able to give the explanations and we shall reserve one item for a general discussion. I think that will be satisfactory.

I would suggest that the large item of $1,300,000 might be the one to be reserved. That is the item really on which the discussion has taken place in the last two years and it practically covers every branch of the militia service. I am sorry my report is not on the table Mr. PATERSON.
but as the militia report is brought up to the end of the calendar year, it was impossible to get it into the printers' hands until about this time. As a matter of fact it has been in the printer's hands for a couple of weeks and I hope to have it in a couple of days.
Would the minister in the meantime explain these items ?

This item of pay and allowances, as will be seen in the detailed statement on page 38, is for pay and allowances of the Headquarters and District Staff, pay of Permanent Corps, pay of officers and men attending Schools of Instruction, allowances to active militia, and guards of honour. There is an increase in the pay of the Headquarters and District Staff of between $8,000 and $9,000. This is due to the fact that some changes have been made at headquarters ; some additional branches have been created, and additional officers appointed. With regard to the second item, the $460,000, there is a very considerable increase.

Before the minister goes on to that he might say what additional officers have been appointed and what additional pay is given to the Headquarters and District Staff. What part of the $9,000 there is for new officers.

There is a Director of Training and Intelligence whose pay is to be $2,800, an Assistant Adjutant General, a Director of Artillery, a Director of Transports and Supplies, a Director of Operations and Staff Duties, a Director of Cloth and Equipment. All these are really changes in name chiefly. There is a new officer, the Director of Operations and Staff Duties at $2,800 and an assistant at $1,700.
Whom have you appointed to these two offices?

They are not filled; we are simply providing for them. I may say in this connection that under the authority of the Act passed last session, a reorganization of the Headquarters Staff has taken place, under the direction chiefly of General Lake, who came from England a month or two ago, and who is Chief of the General Staff. He has'assisted me in constituting a Militia Council under the authority of the Act, and these changes have been made at his suggestion, and with the approval of the Militia Council.

Is that a case of an officer from the old country coming out to succeed one of whom the minister is reported not long since to have said that the chief function of each general officer commanding is to prove that his predecessor was an unwise man. Are not these the changes which were made necessary by the Bill passed last session ?
Yes.

Have the regulations and orders which were to have been submitted to parliament before the Militia Act of last session became law, been passed? If so, might I suggest that the minister have a copy sent to each member of parliament?
Who is the principal medical officer of No. 8 district?
Surgeon-major Bridges.
I saw in one of the daily papers yesterday or the day before that Dr. Bridges had resigned that position, and that Dr. March had been appointed.
I am not aware of such being the case. I will get the information and let my hon. friend know at a later stage.
How are these officers paid?

The Principal Medical Officers in districts where there are permanent depots receive the pay of their rank. While there .are no permanent depots they are paid during the camp, and they are given $25 a month for any duties they may have to perform between the camps.

I see that Major Bridges is put down as receiving only $2 per day for 366 days to June 30, 1904, the whole amount being $732. If he were receiving the pay of his'rank, I should think he would receive more than that.

Yes,, $4 per day would be the pay. I am informed that that was before the permanent appointment was made. Dr. Bridges was then a private practitioner and a surgeon in the active militia, and his services were utilized after the death of Dr. McLearn, I think it was, at the rate mentioned by my hon. friend. I will look into the matter, however. My attention has been called to it now for the first time.
Is he resident in Fredericton and does he attend to the military school there?
Yes.

Is the allowance of so much per month to these principal medical officers supposed to differ from the ordinary pay the militia officers draw for their services while in camp ? In other words, does it constitute them permanent officers or not?

No, it does not. For instance, in my own district, No. 9, in Nova Scotia, there is no depot; but still it is necessary to have the services of 14
a Principal Medical Officer, not only in camp but at other times during the year, and he is obliged to be in almost constant correspondence with the headquarters here. He is called on to make the examinations of men who are going to attend the schools and to render other services, and it was thought only fair to allow him the small fee of $25 a month to indemnify him from loss.
The point I wish to make is this. In case one of these officers should have the chance of being elected to parliament, it will not affect his independence under the Independence of Parliament Act?
No, it is not intended to do so. I think the Independence of Parliament Act specifically protects the militia officer from being affected by any amount of money he receives.

I would like the minister to bring down all the details in connection with the retirement of Colonel Gregory from the command of his regiment, for I can tell him that Colonel Gregory has been illegally retired, and he has a ground of action against the government if he chooses to take it. I have also received some correspondence in relation to Colonel Herchmer. The minister considers that he does not come under his authority; but I believe it was through the Militia Department that he obtained his dismissal. Then, what act did the government take, either through the Canadian authorities or through the imperial authorities, in relation to a Surgeon Devine, at Winnipeg, in regard to his distinguished services, how did he obtain his Distinguished Service Order and on what reports did he obtain them? I would also like the details connected with the proposed reorganization of the 16th glad to give the information required.
Those items will be in ' Hansard ' and I shall be very glad to give the information required.
Will the hon. minister give us some idea of the duties of these new officers, one of whom is receiving $2,800 and the other $1,700 a year ?
This officer, as I understand it, shall have special control over the instructions to be given with reference to the movements of troops in the field.
What is his rank ?

Director of Operations and Staff Duties. He comes immediately under General Lake, the Chief of the General Staff. He should be one of the best qualified men in the service, because the condition of the troops, the knowledge they have of tactical work and the work necessary to make them efficient in



the field, will depend yery largely on the instruction given by this officer. He will direct the officers in command of districts and of camps as to the instruction they
are to give.
<Mr. SAM. HUGHES. Does the hon. minister mean to say that this officer will be superior to the District Officer Commanding ?
Not at all.

Then how will he direct him ?
-Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. Through the regular authority, through the Chief of the General Staff.

If the general staff determines what the duties are to be, why could the instructions not be sent by the secretary ? What is the use of this officer ? The district officer commanding has no right to take orders from a junior officer except as representing his superior.

What I meant to say was that it will be the duty of this officer to study and perfect himself in matters of this kind and to prescribe, suggest and advise. When his advice is accepted, instructions are sent through the proper channel to the different District Officers Commanding districts.
Does the hon. minister suppose that an officer would occupy all his time laying out plans for drill in camp ?	,
There are many other things besides that. There is the Intelligence Department. His business is to look over the whole field where military operations might take place-the whole country.

What will the rank
of this officer be ?
He will not necessarily be of very high rank-a Major, possibly Lieutenant-Colonel. I think the imperial officer to whom the place was offered had the rank of Major.
Why did Col. Denny retire ?
His time was up in April and he was offered a position in the Imperial Service which he would have lost had he remained here. He, therefore, requested to be allowed to go and his request was granted.

It was on his own motion he retired ?
<Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. Entirely.

I am not a military man but belong to the larger proportion of laymen. I understand from the newspapers that we are now to have a military coun-Sir F. W. BORDEN.
cil. That, I suppose, eliminating the minister, will be the highest authority in the administration of the Militia Department. Will the hon. member give us briefly the constitution of that council ? I do not quite see what this training master has to do.

I regret that I am not really in a position to make as clear a statement as I would like to make on this point. I do not think I can do better than read from the regulations we have just passed and which give the scope of the new proposals, copied very largely from what is being done in England. It will be found in the King's Regulations and Orders for the Militia of Canada, 1904, page 205, Appendix A.:
Extract from a report of the Committee of Privy Council approved by the Governor General, 17th November, 1904, as amended by Order -in Council, 17-th December, 1904.
On a report dated 15th November, 1904, from the Minister of Militia and Defence, submitting that by the Militia Act, 1904, section 7, It is enacted -as follows :-
The- Governor in Council may appoint a militia council to advise the minister on all matters relating to the- -militia which are-referred to the council by the minister. The composition, procedure and powers of the council shall be as prescribed.
The minister submits that it is expedient that a militia council he appointed accordingly, and recommends that it be constituted under the title of the militia council and that it be composed of the following members :-
Pres.-The Minister of Militia and D-efe-nce.
First Military member-the chief of the general staff.
Who is lie ?

General Lake. -Second military member, the Adjutant General ; he is Colonel Vidal. Third military member, the Quartermaster General ; he is Colonel Macdonald. Fourth Military member, the Master General of the Ordnance ; he is Colonel Cotton. Civil member, the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence. Finance member, the Accountant of the Department of Militia and Defence, with a secretary to be nominated by the Minister of Militia and Defence from among the clerical staff of this department. Mr. Jarvis has been made secretary.
What position does Lord Aylmer hold ?
He Is Inspector General.
And not on this staff ?
No.
Is he not a member of the council ?

No. Those whose names I have given form the council.

The minister further recommends as regards its procedure.
1.	That the militia council shall meet once a fortnight or oftener, at his direction, for the transaction of business.
2.	That a full, but not necessary verbatim,
account of the proceedings of the council shall be kept by the secretary and printed for record, together with a schedule of the decisions arrived at'.	1
3.	That all such decisions shall be recorded as those of ' The Minister in Militia Council.'
4.	That the business brought before the council may be" any question which the minister may desire to refer for the advice of his council, and, in addition, any matter upon which the member charged with the administration of such matter may wish to obtain the opinion of the council, and the decision of the minister.
Would the hon. minister give a case in explanation of that ?
