2.	Settling the reserves of food, clothing,
equipment, general stores and material to be held in depots, garrisons or mobilization stores, and the scales of such articles to be in possession of the troops.	«
3.	Holding and issuing all military stores.
4.	Administration of the transport, remounts, railway, supply, barrack, ordinance and veterinary services.
5.	Compensation for injuries to men, animals or material.
6.	Selection of officers for employment in the above services.
7.	Administration of the ordinance store corps.
8.	Arrangements for postal services.
it. Advising and assisting the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence in making arrangements for contracts for the above services.
10. Preparation, jointly with the finance member, of estimates for the above services.

The master-general of the ordnance, as fourth military member, shall be charged with:
1.	The armament of the forces, including mines, electric lights and all accessories.
2.	Sites, designs and armaments for the permanent defences.
3.	Settling scales of reserves of arms and ammunition of all kinds.
4.	Patterns, provision and inspection of guns, small arms, ammunition and artillery and engineer technical stores and vehicles.
5.	Inspection of the process of manufacture in the ordnance factories and control of ordnance workshops.
6.	Instruction and maintenance of fortifications, artillery and rifle ranges. Preparation of general plans for all military buildings.
7.	Maintenance of barracks and military-buildings ar.d lands in military occupation.
Does the minister build these buildings, or is that work in charge of the Department of Public Works ?
The relative positions of the Department of Public Works and the Department of Militia are not changed in any way. Our work is limited to repairs and to the purely military structures.
Is he recognized by the Public Works as an officer of the Public Works Department, who had the duty of making plans for military buildings ?
No.
Then he only has advisory power ?
That is all.
Suppose a subordinate officer should submit plans of a buildIng, would the Public Works construct them as the Minister of Militia wished ?

We ascertain what the requirements are, and submit to the Department of Public Works a state-Sir F. W. BORDEN.
ment of our requirements. They make a plan and return that plan to us ; if we have any criticism to make we make the criticism and return the plan to the Public Works. There are frequent conferences between the Engineer in charge of this work in the Militia Department and the Architect in the Public Works Department.
Have you no architect in the Militia Department ?
We have now hi the Engineering Branch.

Do I understand the minister to say that this ordnance officer has control of the manufacture of small arms ? For instance, would he have supervision of the ammunition at present being manufactured in Quebec, and of the Ross rifle, and that sort of thing ?

He would control the inspection. He has the right to go into these factories at any moment and see what is going on, to have a report of the work that is being done there, to see it himself, and to have samples of the ammunition which is being manufactured. So far as rifles are concerned, the inspection of small arms will be directly under his control.

In the event of any defect being discovered in the small arms and ammunition, or in the rifle itself, with whom would the rectification of this fault lie ? Would he look after that himself, or would it be submitted to the council or a body of experts ?

I should think it would be submitted to the Council. But the Master of Ordnance is primarily responsible for these things being properly done. He is responsible for the inspection, there is no question about that. We are now considering a board of inspection, but that has not been done yet.

In this connection I might suggest to the minister-I have no right to make a motion to this effect-hut there has been from time to time, as he well knows, very grave questions arising as to whether this officer was acting within his authority. For instance, I claim that Colonel Gregory has not been dismissed from the service, although his name has been struck off the list. He is illegally dismissed, and I intend to bring up that question before the end of the session. Now I was hoping that the minister would have brought down an estimate this year for a judge advocate general. He has in his department an officer admirably qualified for that position. I mean Colonel Smith ; and in case he would not take the position, I believe it is possible to find another officer in Canada of great legal ability and broad training who would take that position. Al-

though the department has not lost a great deal in lawsuits they might have lost a great deal if persons who have a right to complain against the action of officers had followed up their complaints. I hope the minister will have a judge advocate general appointed.	1

There is a great deal of force in what my hon. friend says, and that proposition is now under consideration by the Council, and before the end of the session the House may be asked to vote the sum necessary. I will now continue with the enumeration of the duties of the Master General of the Ordnance, the fourth military member of the board, so far as we have worked them out:
8.	Administration of the engineer staff employed in the above works.
9.	Personnel of the technical inspection staff.
10.	Technical instruction at artillery and engineer schools and courses.
11.	Technical artillery and engineer questions.
12.	Preparation, jointly with the finance member, of estimates for the above services.
13.	Advising and assisting the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence in making contracts for guns, ammunition, and works constructed under his1 control.
I did not quite understand the minister in answer to my question as to who would he responsible in case of any defect being found in the small arms and ammunition.
The Master General of Ordnance.
Would he have a staff of experts to decide whether they were effective ?

Perhaps he would not be able to decide himself, although he is a man of technical knowledge in such matters, and one of the best qualified officers we have in Canada. But he would have the assistance of men technically qualified. For instance, at Quebec he would have in his employ a chemist of first rate capacity, whose services would be required to test the character of the cordite and a number of things that are used in the manufacture of the cartridge. But in any case when there is a complaint of the inferior character of the ammunition, it is always made to the minister, who would at once bring the matter to the attention of the Militia Council and of the officers specially charged with that duty.

I ask these question because at one of the rifle ranges last season there was a suspicion that the ammunition was not what it should have been, whether through defect in the manufacture or not, I cannot say. It is a very important mattei- upon whicoa lives of men may depend. It is a question whether the Master General of Ordnance is able to supervise
thoroughly himself, without the aid of qualified experts, the manufacture of ammunition and of the new rifle which I believe is about to be adopted.
'Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. The Master General of Ordnance will have the assistance of the best technical knowledge that we can provide, and if it is not to be had here we will send away and get it. 1 am very glad the hon. gentleman has brought the question up and I will he pleased to hear from him in detail privately, if he likes, or he may write me. a letter in reference to the particular occasions on which this failure in the ammunition was found to exist. I am told that the same trouble occurs in England. It is absolutely impossible to have the ammunition uniformly and always good. I am also told that our percentage of imperfections is not greater than it is in England.
It is all tested before it is issued, is it not ?
Yes, samples are tested. It canuot all be tested, of course. You cannot test it till you use it, but a certain percentage of the cartridges that are made every day are tested.
Would it be in order to ask the hon. minister if the department had any adverse reports in regard to the Ross rifle V
No, I am not aware of any adverse reports. There has been some question as to the sight but it has beeu changed and improved.
Was there not some imperfection in regard to the breach?

Not that I am aware of. Of course I am only speaking of my own personal knowledge. I have now come to the deputy minister.
The Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, as civil member, shall be charged with :
1.	The interior economy of the Militia Department.
2.	The administration of non-effective votes.
3.	Parliamentary business and reports to council.
4.	Formal communication to other departments of state1.
5.	The preparation of papers for submission to the militia council, of official reports of its proceedings, and record of the decisions taken.
6.	The 'administration of contracts, in consultation, with the branches specially concerned.
7.	Arrangements for the construction of new barracks and other buildings.
In the case of new barracks to he constructed for instance at Montreal, the deputy minister would carry out the business part of it. The work is really done by the Department of Public Works, but the deputy head of the department would carry

out any business negotiations in reference to the construction of these barracks.
8.	The custody of militia lands not in military occupation' and purchase- of land for military purposes.
9.	Such other business as the minister may allot to him1.
In the absence of the Minister of Militia, he will act for him in all matter of ordinary business.
The hon. Minister of Agriculture will not act any more?
You will have to ask him.

The hon. Minister of Militia and Defence says that the deputy minister has charge of the purchase and selection of lands for military purposes including the purchase of sites for drill sheds. I will cite a little case that happened in my district. We were very anxious to have a new drill shed at Sherbrooke to replace the old one which existed in the vicinity of the parade ground, the only available place for drill purposes in the city, and several deputations waited upon the Minister of Militia and Defence, or his predecessor, in respect to the purchase of a site adjoining this parade ground. Nothing was done until finally an officer landed in Sherbrooke one day, who, in company with a noted publican who was a warm supporter of the government, drove about the city and on his advice purchased a tract of land which was far distant from this parade ground and which was not suitable for a drill shed. It was a site which the militia did not want and about which they were not consulted at all ; in fact, the officer came down and in connection with this hotel keeper purchased this piece of land for the purpose of a drill shed. It was not until shortly before he was leaving on the afternoon train that he had the courtesy to call on the senior officer of that town and tell him what he was down there for. In spite of all the representations which have been made to the department, they have still persisted in retaining this land as the proposed site for the new drill shed. As the hon. minister knows several deputations have waited upon him and not on him alone but on the hon. Minister of Agriculture as well. I think I was a member of one of these deputations, and while I do not mean to say that the hon. Minister of Agriculture would entirely usurp the functions of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, I think that on that occasion he had everything to say to us. He went so far as to tell us that if this drill shed site did not suit us we could do what we liked about it, in fact if the proposed site did not suit our regiment it would do for another which might be formed. I think that matters in connection with the selection of a site for a drill shed should not be left entirely with the Deputy Minister of Militia Sir F. W. BORDEN.
and Defence or with any one man. If you have an engineer, or an architect, or anybody who is competent and knows how to select sites of that kind he is the man who should be entrusted with the performance of that duty, but at the same time I think he should be instructed to consult with the officers in the district when buildings of this sort are to be erected. I think that the system of leaving the selection of a site of that kind entirely in the hands of one man is open to serious objection.

It does not follow because there has been this division of work that the particular things placed under particular officers are solely under the control of those officers. Not at all. They all come under the purview of the Militia Council, under the minister and finally under the Governor in Council. As far as the particular case which my hon. friend refers to is concerned, if he were not a young member of the House, I would say that he was rather out of order in bringing it in here at this moment. It is hardly apropos because the deputy minister, as a matter of fact, is not the officer who went there. The course pursued is this :	An officer of the
Headquarters Staff, the Quartermaster General or the Adjutant General-the QuarterMaster General, I think-is sent to the locality where the building is to be constructed and is asked to make a report.
Now an officer is not able to purchase. My hon. friend says that this officer, whoever he was, went down and drove around with some one whom he does not approve of, and that he purchased a piece of land. I do not know what he means by saying that this officer drove around publicly ; whether he means to insinuate that it had any effect upon the officer's report or not, but as a matter of fact the officer who went down had no power to purchase; he did not purchase. He made a report to me-there was not a Militia Council then-with regard to certain lands available. I met several deputations of the citizens and officers of Sherbrooke, and alter listening very carefully to the mayor of tne city and other influential gentlemen, including a gentleman of the name of Col. Worthington, of that city, I came to the conclusion that the site recommended by this officer was a good and satisfactory site, I recommended it to the Governor General in Council, and an order in council was passed authorizing the purchase of this site. I have not the papers here, it is a very inconvenient moment to discuss this matter, but 'if my hon. friend wishes to discuss it I shall be very glad to bring down the papers later on and to discuss it as fully as may be necessary.	.

The minister undertook to read the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Worthington) a lesson, and to intimate that he had violated the rules of the House or the rules of debate in bringing up this particular

matter at this particular time. I wish to say that in my opinion-and I am sure in yours also Mr. Clnfirman, and yours will have more weight in this house than mine, because of your official position-that the hon. member for Sherbrooke was not at all out of order in bringing up this particular matter at this particular time, because we are discussing the appointment of an officer who would be charged with the particular duty of going about the country and selecting sites when necessary. What more lit-ing time could the hon. member have chosen in which to bring this up ?

I wish to call the attention of the minister to the fact that the deputation, of which my brother, Lt. Col. E. B. Worthington was a member, did not call on him to discuss the drill shed site, but to discuss the camp ground. Whether that question was brought up at that time or not I do not know, but the deputation were certainly not sent in connection with the drill shed on that occasion, but only in connection with the camp ground. As the minister does not understand what the connection was between the officer who visited Sherbrooke to select a drill shed site and this party to whom I refer, I may say that when this officer went to Sherbrooke he must have had some definite object and some instructions. What were his instructions ? To whom was he to report ? Was he to go around and pick out the first available site he saw or was he to go to some one who had some pull and ask for his advice as to where he should locate a drill shed ? It seems to me he must have gone there with the intention of going directly to this man, because I understand that he was met at the station and spent the day with him and reported to nobody in Sherbrooke. Certainly it would have been an act of courtesy not only on the part of the visiting officer, but on the part oi the department too if that officer had seen the military officers in charge of that locality.

Whilst this question is fresh would the minister take into consideration one thing which if carried out would, in my opinion, be a most excellent thing for his department. The case cited by the hon. member for Sherbrooke illustrates it exactly. If any bodyr of men in a town should be aole to form a good opinion as to where a drill shed site should be it would be the men who have interest enough in military matters to form a company and carry on drill at great expense and with great trouble. If the minister would make this selecting of drill shed sites, once and for all, entirely non-partisan, and have in view simply what is best for the militia of that district, putting out of view entirely what this man or that man who may be interested because he has something to'sell would like to have done for his own personal or political advantage, and to have in view simply the suitability and fitness of a site he would do a good thing for
the militia, for his own department and for himself as an administrator in that department. I have heard of so many cases of wrong selection that have taken place, not only' with respect to military sites, but also with respect to post offices, and public building sites, that I think we are surely old enough, wise enough and strong enough to select these sites simply because of adaptability and suitability for the purpose for which they are intended. I am quite sure that the Deputy Minister of Militia, if he were left to himself, would prefer this. A deputy has no political leanings. He has no business to permit the least iota of a tinge of partisanship or political bias to influence his discharge of the duties of his office. If any political considerations are to be regarded that is the duty of the minister and not of the deputy minister, and you have the most useful deputy minister when you leave him entirely free from the trammel of partisanship or political bias. I am quite sure that if the Deputy Minister of Militia were left free to exercise his judgment he would make these selections perfectly well, honestly and fairly. Let us eliminate a little of this small partisanship and have these sites selected on the ground of suitability for the prupose.
I endorse every word that my hon. friend has said. While I am not going to admit-I do not think it would be correct to make an admission-that in this particular case any improper act is done.
We do not want any admissions.	[DOT]

Still I believe in the selection of sites for public buildings perhaps, both under former administrations and under this administration, too much attention has been paid to political influences. I think that the establishment of the Militia Council will enable the minister, who is genuinely anxious to act in the interest of the public, to act independently and properly and fairly. One of my objects in desiring the establishment of this Council was to be relieved, as far as possible, of any influence, political, social or otherwise, which might be used against the public interest in coming to a determination as to the selection of sites or otherwise. I am glad to know that my hon. friend takes the view he does and I hope he will stand by me in the independent carrying out of this idea.
It will be a great wrench to stand by you, but I will do it on this, sure.

When these mlli-| tary properties are taken over by the depart. ment, under the control of which of these J officers will they come?
- Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. The Quarter ' Master General.
Then, why not make him the responsible officer for selecting the sites?

He has been. Because a certain duty has been allotted to a certain officer as being more properly within his scope, it does not follow that he has absolute control. As a matter of fact, all these things come before the Council, and in the future no selection of a drill site or a rifle range site will be made without the question being submitted to the Council.

If I am in order in referring to the grounds which have been allotted to the Ross Rifle Company, I would like to state that about the end of November last, I was in Quebec with a number of visitors who were strangers to the place. We walked out to the Plains of Abraham, and as we did so thp. first thing that attracted our attention, and that was in evidence more than anything else, was an immense water tank erected on the top of one of the old Martello towers, the legs being driven through the tower, and the water tank standing sixty or seventy feet in the air, the one hideous thing on the landscape. If there was no sentiment about the place, it would be ugly enough; but the rifle buildings themselves are about as ugly as they can be, and a little further on this hideous water tower. It looks as if there were some sort of plan to destroy all the beauty and interest in the Plains of Abraham or the approach to them. I may say that the gentlemen jvho were with me, some of them on their first visit to Quebec, came away with the feeling that their visit had been spoiled because of the absolute want of appreciation by the people of Canada of the place and its suroundings. Surely it is not necessary to have such a hideous eye-sore erected there to ruffle the feelings of everybody who goes to look at that historic place.

I am very sorry that my hon. friend's aesthetic taste and poetic feelings and those of his friends have been shocked in this rude manner. I have not seen the water tank, so far as I remember, but it is true that permission was given to Sir Charles Ross to place a tank in that Martello tower in order to enable him to protect his factory against fire.
I did not understand that the structure was to be one so hideous and disagreeable in appearance, or I certainly should have insisted on some precaution being taken against that. I understood that it would not be visible from the outside at all.

Why, the legs are through the roof of the tower, and there is an erection sixty or seventy feet high, the ugliest possible mercantile tank put on top of it. If that does not destroy the view, you might just as well suggest that a tank should be put on the top of St. Paul's Cathedral or Sir F. W. BORDEN.
the Tower of London, and not do damage to the surroundings. This is sentiment, it is true, but sentiment shrely has something to do with the things of this world; and 1 can tell the minister that, little sentiment as he appears to have, if he goes down to Quebec and looks at that object, he will certainly order it to be taken down. Not a visitor will go to the Plains of Abraham who will not curse the man who put it up. It is so hideous and such an eyesore that I wonder that the citizens of Quebec have not torn it down.
We felt that it was a very desirable thing to have an industry such as that established by the Ross Company.
I agree with that, but I do not think it should be put there.

And even if a Martello tower has been a little disfigured, I think we shall have to try to put up with it. But as my hon. friend has referred to the matter, I will see if we cannot induce the Ross Company to make some changes. They might perhaps put the legs out of sight. Now, I want to finish reading these regulations :
The accountant of the Department of Militia and Defence, as finance member, shall be charged with :-
1.	The consideration and compilation in concert with the various branches co|ncern<ed, of the annual estimates for militia services.
2.	The review of contracts and administration-of the Militia Accountant's Branches.
3.	General consideration of the cost of the militia.
4.	Financial advice to the several branches of the department.
5.	Audit of military accounts.
The minister further recommends that the distribution of duties of the officers of the headquarter's staff, approved by the Governor General in Council on the 29th October, 1903, be cancelled. .
Tbat is,, briefly, tbe construction of the militia council. I may say tbat there Is a regulation describing lu detail tbe duties of these officers. I am sorry that I have not that here, but J will lay it on the table of the House at the earliest possible moment.
I am sure it will give in concise language a better idea of the different duties than I can. I think I have read enough to show that we have framed a very careful constitution for this Militia Council and have included therein all the important branches necessary in the public interest for the earning out of au efficient militia service.

You have these four military heads in the council and two civilian heads. You say that each one advises with the accountant in making up the estimates for the sums necessary to carry out the work assigned to him. How do you work out that system ? Will you have a separate staff under each one of these heads ?

Sir FREDERICK; BORDEN. That is [what has been done.
So that, for instance, your General Master of Ordnance will have under him a special staff to carry out his work ?
Exactly.
What staff has the deputy minister ?
He is the permanent head of the civil branch, and has his clerical staff as before.
Then you will need quite an addition to your working force ?

No, not a very large addition. In fact, on the civil side there is no addition. On the military side there will be some additions, but not many, because we have been able to change around the officers in such a way that no very serious addition will result. The addition amounts to $8,200 for three or foul officers.
Take the four military heads, will each one of those carry out what is assigned to him without having reference to any other head, or to the council as a consultative body ?

He must go before the Council with any important question. I think that that is embodied in the regulations. It is of the first importance that the Minister in Council should have the advantage of hearing the discussions with reference to the different questions about which he may not be informed, and upon which it is absolutely necessary he should be informed. I may say, for the information of my hon. friend, that agenda are prepared a week or two ahead for the information of the Council, and are sent to every member of the Council, so that every one will know what is going to be considered at the next meeting.
So that, practically, the minister, in consulting these officers, is merely carrying out what he formerly did individually ?
Yes.
It is the one mode of communicating between these officers and the minister ?	[DOT]
Precisely.
Where does the Director General of the Medical Service come in ?
Under the Adjutant General.

This is one of the most important branches of the service. The Director General of * Medical Services should certainly be a member of that council. The health of the troops and the sanitation of military camps are of such importance that it seems only reasonable the Sergeant General or Director General of Medical Services should be a member of that council.

The Council calls before it the directors of the different branches. Whenever an important question comes up on which the Council is not fully informed, those officers come before it, or they may request to be heard before it, and their request is always granted.
Apart from that, the medical officer is entitled to a seat in that council. Proper attention is not shown to medical officers. They should have as high rank as any other except the Adjutant General.

While I do not yield to my hon. friend in my respect for the importance of the profession to which both he and I belong, still w'e modelled our system on the British, and in the British Army Council there is no medical officer.
The British Army Council is open to improvement.
We could not put them all on. We made the best selection we could, and I think the fined ical service will not suffer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I have listened very 'patiently to the minister explaining the duties of the board. He wound up by defining the accountant's duty, and said he thought every precaution was taken to guard the public interest. I am not a military man, and am not looking at this matter from a military standpoint at all, but with the eye of a business man, and I do not see in the constitution of this board any provision for the proper laying out of the people's money in purchasing supplies. Let me just draw to the attention of the hon. minister certain items in the Auditor General's Report. Take page V-25, purchased for the Montreal harbour improvements below St. Maurice current, Portland cement, 600 barrels at $1.80. Every one who knows anything about cement knows that Portland cement is the best and most expensive we can get. Then turn up page Q-61. and you will find that the purchasing officer of the Minister of Militia, whoever he may have been, went to Mr. J. B. Jinchereau and bought 19 barrels of cement for improvements in the city of Quebec at $3 and 86 barrels at $2,50
Then he went to Mr. Larose and bought 5 barrels at $3 and 52 barrels at $2.50. Then he went to Mr. Louis Larose and bought 17 barrels at $3 and 86 barrels at $2.50. From Mr. Leon Magnan he purchased 6 barrels at $3 and 98i barrels at $2.50. Thfen he went to Mr. Parent and purchased 75 barrels at $2.50 and 20 barrels at $3. From

another Mr. Parent, Pierre Parent, he purchased 35 barrels at $2.50 and 15 barrels at $3. From 51r. Renaud he bought 141 barrels at $2.50. In all, he bought 98 barrels at $3, 658 barrels at $2.50, and 237 barrels at $2.25. If he had bought all this at the rate which it could be bought In Montreal, $1.80, he would have saved the public not less than $702.05 on these few barrels of cement alone. I have brought these things to the attention of the government year after year, and still they send around in this manner buying these things and paying two prices. The cement for sale in Montreal at $1.80 was Portland cement, which as everybody knows, is the best brand manufactured. There is nothing to show what kind this other was-it may have been mere common cement and not worth half the price. Portland cement is imported and it ought to be landed at Quebec or Halifax as cheap or cheaper than at Montreal. I hope the minister, will arrange to have the supplies for the Militia Department bought under conditions of public competition, so that the public may be able to get the goods at bottom prices. This board should have a purchasing department, and let the board itself decide how these supplies should be bought in the best interests of the country. At page 67 the hon. minister will find that a bill as paid to Mr. N. E. Keefer of $3,183.56. Among the items is one for repairing roof of armouries, painting walls, &c., labourers 146 days at $3.50, and 53i days at $3.25. and masons and slaters are paid at 45 cents an hour. It seems to me that $3.50 is a very big price for labouring men in Halifax.
Halifax came high all the way through-the minister knows that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then I find at page Q-66, they charge for 32 cedar posts at $1 a piece. Unless they are carved or something of that kind I cannot understand how they cost so much. This was at Annapolis, Nova Scotia. If there were the ordinary posts that we buy at 20 cents a piece in Ontario, I do not see why they should cost so much at Annapolis. I hope the minister will take down these figures and give us an explanation of them.

As to the cedar posts I have paid $1 a piece for an extra quality of post myself-a post that would square 7 inches. I shall be glad to make inquiry into the matters to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has called attention. As to the cement, I fancy the price varies with the time and place and also witli the quantity purchased. The Auditor General must have passed this account, and I do not imagine that he would have passed it if there had been anything seriously wrong. However, as to the general question which these items are used to illustrate, I agree with the hon. gentleman that it would be a proper matter for discussion by the Mr. TAYLOR.
Militia Council. As a matter of fact, I have already mentioned the matter and it is being considered by the Council with a view to adopting a plan under which the best results in the public interest may be attained in the purchase of supplies. These purchases cannot be always made by tender, but, so far as that can be done, it ought to be done. I have brought the matter before the council, and I hope that before the session is over I shall be able to submit the plan they have adopted.

A few moments ago we were talking about the Plains of Abraham. Will the minister please say how many acres there are in the government's purchase, what portion of it has been leased to certain parties for a factory site and whether the rumours are true that the government intend to dispose of the whole property ?

I do not think there is any truth in the rumour that the government intend to dispose of the property. I have never heard it even proposed. I am not able to give the size of this property, but I will ascertain it. The quantity leased to the Ross Company is not large-in fact not large enough; for they are asking for more.	[DOT]
Is it part of the Plains?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is within a few acres of the Citadel, between the Martello towers which, as the hon. gentleman is aware, are on the top of what we call Per-rault's Hill, the highest point west of the city, and the citadel. We call it the Old Cove Fields.
What are the dimensions of the Plains ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe it has been proven that what we have hitherto considered the Plains of Abraham is not the Plains of Abraham at all. It is a mile away from the Plains of Abraham. If the hon. gentleman is acquainted with the locality, it is on the other side of the road from the parliament buildings, behind a block of houses, about two acres to the west on the other side of St. Louis Street.
Where is that Martello tower?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Martello tower is to the south, that is the one immediately over the cliff.

There was a disposition to laugh at my hon. friend from Toronto when he spoke about that, but I do not think it is a laughing matter at all. There are impressions that our own people get, and impressions that visitors get, that have a great influence upon our future. I think we ought to have some regard for aesthetics, and keep what we have got in
that line and treasure it particularly. Take one of those old historic landmarks about which so much has been written,and around which so many memories cluster; we find our own people visit them with the idea of history in their minds, prizing the oid landmarks, and people come there from abroad with the same idea, but when they come into the actual presence of one of them they see a great big pair of legs protruding with a tank set up on top. It is an unsightly thing, and ought not to have been allowed. The factory's water tank should go somewhere else, and leave the Martello tower as one of the few landmarks we have in this country, a thing of beauty and a joy forever.

The Directors are assistants of the military members, they are in charge of the important subdivisions of the work of the different branches I have read. For instance, in the department of the Master General of Ordnance we have engineering as one of the important branches of his department. The Director of Engineering is under him and the Director of Engineering again has officers under him. Then artillery is naturally one of the important branches of the duties of the Master General of Ordnance and under him also we have a Director of Artillery, an officer who has been in Canada for some time. But there are exceptions in favour of the service dress. This is a pretty serious matter. In the rural corps

I admit that.
The understanding is that an officer at a function should either go in the proper uniform of his corps-that is, dress uniform-or, if it is a superior function, he should go in evening dress.

I think one of the reasons for this mixture of uniforms to which my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) refers is due to the fact that he may have seen officers of the regular service in company with those of a corps of guides dressed in khaki.

I have seen officers of the 65th battalion, some dressed in khaki and some dressed in their ordinary uniforms. I have also seen some of the high officials there, some dressed in khaki and some in ordinary uniform.
Staff officers ?
Staff officers ; and the result is that one who is not very well posted is at a loss to know what their rank is.
Well, I think that is undesirable.

At the same time,
I would be sorry to see an officer obliged to go to the cost of providing himself with mess uniform. A young officer, a young chap with a small salary, perhaps not more than enough to keep him, should not be obliged to go to the expense of purchasing an expensive mess uniform. He should go to a function in evening dress.
That would be all right if they were all on the same footing.

When a regimental function takes place, and the officer in command of the regiment has not all his officers properly uniformed, the custom is for them to wear undress uniforms, so that all will be alike.

If that were the rule, it would put an end to any difficulty in regard to the matter.

The reason I asked about the camps is that I would think it very desirable, especially where cavalry-form the main branch of the service, as for example in the Eastern Townships, where we have the Eastern Townships Cavalry Brigade, to have the drill take place near the local headquarters. For several years back these mounted corps have been entrained at the different headquarters and taken by various trains down to Doucet's Landing, put on the ferry and taken across to Three Rivers, and the cost of transport for these mounted infantry corps is far greater than the cost of their whole term in camp. I think it would be far better to have these cavalry regiments drill in the country to which they- belong. In the Eastern Townships we are right on the frontier and it is very essential that these men should know the country which they are expected to defend, know the railroads, and rivers and bridges and for that reason I think it would be far better for them to drill in their own districts. Those who do not live in the immediate vicinity of the camp grounds could march into camp instead of being entrained. No corps there would be far enough away to necessitate entraining in order to get to camp, and a day's march coming in and going out would

be very instructive on account of tbe route march, and the possible bivouacking and camping and the stops for meals and feed. This is a very essential part of the training. For instance in connection with the Eastern Township Cavalry Brigade, I think it essential that a camp should be held at a central point, say the headquarters of the brigade, Sherbrooke, which is right on the frontier. A number of very important railroads centre there, while there are many railroads within from 12 to 30 miles of that place, all along the frontier, which these men should know and be able to protect in case of actual warfare.
*Sir I''Rill)ERICK BORDEN. No doubt there is considerable force in what my hon. friend says, but at the same time I would point out to him that in case of active service the cavalry would be serving with infantry and artillery, and it is desirable I think, to bring the different arms of the service together in the camps, so that they may understand in some degree at least the relationship which they bear to each other in active service. As to my hon. friend's statement with reference to the cost of going to Three Rivers, he is altogether at sea in stating that the cost of transportation is greater than the full cost of the camp. It is really nothing of the kind, as I can show him at any time. Three Rivers was selected some time ago, very largely owing to the fact that an outbreak of smallpox had occurred among the Indians at La Prairie, where we had been holding a camp for some years. The Director General of Medical Affairs reported that it was absolutely unsafe, and it meant either having no camp or finding another location. A very favourable location was offered to us at Three Rivers at a low figure; and the city of Three Rivers offered light, water and various inducements, and the camp has been held there for two or three years. Last year we had a camp at Laprairie and one at Three Rivers also. I do not know where the camp will be held this year, but I am sure the Council will give every considera-ation to the question.
Why were the cavalry drilled last year at Laprairie and the infanty at Three Rivers if it is so essential that the various branches be drilled together ?
Does my hon. friend deny that it is essential to have the different branches of the service drilled together ?
No, I think it is very essential that they should be drilled together, but there is no place at Three Rivers where artillery can be drilled or where you can manoeuvre cavalry.

Dominion Arsenal, $150,000.
Is there more than one factory now?
No, only one.
Is it the intention of the minister to establish another?
Yes.
How soon?

I hope before very long. I explained last year, and I think something was said about it the year before, that there were some people in this country and in England-they have taken out articles of incorporation since-interested in the establishment of a factory for the manufacture of ammunition ; and a condition will be imposed by the government that in case this is done, they shall manufacture in this country all the explosives necessary to be used for the manufacture of ammunition, both in their factory and in the government factory at Quebec. The matter is taking shape, and I hope before the end of the session to be able to lay on the table further information with reference to it, and possibly a contract.
Then, do I understand that it would be the intention of the government to abandon the manufacture ?

Not at all. We want to have more factories for the manufacture of ammunition. Practically the only factory in Canada now is in the government arsenal at Quebec. It is desirable that ammunition should be manufactured at several points, certainly somewhere in the vicinity of Ottawa. I think it is equally desirable that we should manufacture in Canada all the explosives that are used now, in our factory at Quebec, which are at present imported. I would not propose to give a contract to any company for the manufacture of ammunition which would not also undertake to manufacture explosives.
In my opinion it is inadvisable to hand over the manufacture of ammunition to any private company. I think the ammunition should be manufactured by the government itself.
That is not done in England.

I do not care what is done in England; that is not necessarily a
precedent for us. I think the ammunition should be manufactured solely by the government itself, so as to guard against the danger of its being faulty.

I am afraid that would be a pretty expensive operation, and I have felt that it would be an advantage to encourage a private company to manufacture ammunition as a sort of check upon our own factory. That is what is done in the United States as well as in England. The government manufactures a part and the trade manufactures a part, and one is a sort of check on the other. The present seems to me a favourable moment for encouraging the manufacture of explosives in this country, when we are about to enter upon the construction of railways, perhaps to a greater extent than ever before, and large quantities of explosives will be required ; and it is a moment when private capital may be induced to go into the venture. But I can assure you that I have had very great difficulty in satisfying private capital that there will be any money in going into the manufacture of explosives for government use only, it would be such a very small quantity.

It might not be a bad idea to establsh these powder factories in connection with the penitentiaries. In case anything happened, the loss of life would not be so important.
'Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. That would be better than manufacturing binder twine.

When the minister brings down his budget of information, there is some information which I would like, and which probably the country would like as well. I would like to know just about what is the military equipment of Canada to-day -how many drilled militia we have, how many rifles we have for them, what stores of ammunition, what large guns, what fortifications, if any, looking towards the protection of our sea-board cities, we have. That indicates the kind of information I would like to get so far as it can be given without injuring our strategical position. I want to say this, that if we are pretty naked, as I think we are, I think it- would not do much harm to confess that we are, and let outsiders see simply our brawny arms, provided we make up our minds to do better things and put ourselves in a stronger position. I think we are living on rather slender resources for the defence of this country, and if our people understood the exact position we are in, you might find a larger number ready to support any measures necessary to be taken for the proper defence and equipment of the country.

I am very glad to find my hon. friend taking a greater interest in matters of this kind than perhaps any of us took a few years ago. I might

point out that there is some information which can he given out, but other information with regard to guns and rifles or location of ammunition which I think it undesirable to give. I would suggest that a committee of kon. gentlemen from both sides might meet me or the Council and learn exactly what the conditions are. If my hon. friend who leads the opposition will consider that suggestion I shall be very glad to have a number of gentlemen who take an interest in the matter meet the council and get all the information that can be afforded.
That is a good idea. You have to get the people to acknowledge that there is a want before you get their support.

If that suggestion were carried out it would mean that those composing the committee would be bound to secrecy and we could not take any advantage from a conference of that kind. There was a good deal of difference of opinion expressed last year on this point and regarding the publication of the Major General's report. Many military men, including the major general himself, thought that the report should have been submitted to the House in order that the members might know what an officer of the high character and ability of Lord Dundonald considered necessary for the defence of the country. Was any portion of the $110,000 voted for defences at Esquimau paid the British authorities ?

The whole of it was paid to the British authorities. There is an arrangement between the British government and this government with reference to payments for the expense of defending Esquimau. Under that arrangement we divide the expenditure. The British government has charge of it and employs its own men very largely except during the annual camp once a year, and we reimburse it one half the expense.
I understood that a year or two ago our share was $35,000. Has it increased?
A new arrangement was made three or four years ago and laid on the table, under which we pay half the costs.
This is every dollar that Canada contributes to the defense of the country from an Imperial point of view?

No ; the
Canadian government has paid considerable money for the purchase of sites for large guns. We paid $25,000 last year. That was a part of the agreement. We buy all the land necessary for the mounting of the necessary guns for defence.
